question: How long before bed should caffeine be stopped to protect sleep?
keyResult: Caffeine reduced total sleep time by 45 min and sleep efficiency by 7%, increased sleep onset latency by 9 min and wake after sleep onset by 12 min, and reduced deep sleep (N3/N4) by 11.4 min (-1.4%). To avoid reductions in total sleep time, coffee (107 mg per 250 mL) should be consumed at least 8.8 h before bedtime, and a standard pre-workout supplement (217.5 mg) at least 13.2 h before bedtime.

citation.title: The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Gives a longer cutoff than Drake 2013 (6 h). For a 10-11 p.m. bedtime, 8.8 h means about 1-2 p.m., which fits 'early afternoon' better than a 4 p.m. cutoff. A larger dose (217.5 mg) needs 13.2 h, i.e. morning only.
notes: Authors declare no conflicts. Mostly lab studies in healthy, often young, adults; cutoff scales with dose, so a single clock time is a simplification.

question: Does caffeine taken 0, 3 or 6 hours before bed disturb sleep?
keyResult: 400 mg caffeine taken at bedtime, 3 h before, or 6 h before bedtime each significantly disturbed sleep compared with placebo (p < 0.05 for all). The authors conclude caffeine 6 h before bed has important disruptive effects and support refraining from substantial caffeine for a minimum of 6 hours before bedtime.

citation.title: Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed.

disagreement: Source of the common '6 hours' rule. Because 6 h still disrupted sleep, 6 h is a minimum, not a safe point; consistent with Gardiner 2023's 8.8 h.
notes: Single high dose (400 mg, roughly 4 cups of coffee). Sample size not stated in abstract; small crossover study.

question: Does the effect of caffeine on sleep depend on age and dose?
keyResult: Caffeine reduced total sleep time (MD = -34.67 min), sleep efficiency (MD = -4.74 %) and slow-wave sleep % (MD = -1.01 %) and prolonged sleep onset latency (MD = +8.35 min); REM% was not significantly affected. Both high- and low-dose caffeine reduced total sleep time and sleep efficiency; meta-regression found no significant linear relationship with continuous age or dose.

citation.title: Age- and dose-specific effects of caffeine on sleep: A meta-analysis of controlled crossover trials.

notes: No competing interests declared. Acute single-dose lab trials; not about habitual intake timing.

question: Do coffee and caffeine harm sleep?
population: epidemiological studies and RCTs, mostly male Western adults
keyResult: Caffeine typically prolonged sleep latency, reduced total sleep time and sleep efficiency, and worsened perceived sleep quality; slow-wave sleep was typically reduced. Dose- and timing-response relationships were established. Older adults may be more sensitive, and genetic differences in adenosine-related genes contribute to individual sensitivity.

citation.title: Coffee, caffeine, and sleep: A systematic review of epidemiological studies and randomized controlled trials.

notes: Supports a note that sensitivity varies by person and age: 'if you are sensitive, stop earlier'.

question: Which modifiable dietary factors are linked to adolescent sleep?
keyResult: Adolescents with higher caffeine intake had increased odds of sleep problems (OR = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.28-2.17), and alcohol consumption was associated with insomnia (OR = 1.17, 95% CI: 1.07-1.27). Healthy foods were consistently linked with better sleep, and fat-, sugar-rich, red or processed foods with poorer sleep.

citation.title: Modifiable dietary factors in adolescent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Adolescents only; mostly cross-sectional and self-reported, so association not causation. No competing interests declared.

question: How do dose and timing of alcohol affect night-time sleep in healthy adults?
keyResult: Alcohol delayed REM sleep onset and reduced REM duration. REM disruption occurred after a low dose (≤0.50 g/kg, approximately two standard drinks) and worsened with increasing dose. Shorter sleep onset latency and latency to deep sleep (N3) were only seen after a high dose (≥0.85 g/kg, approximately five standard drinks). Effects on total sleep time, sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset were too uncertain to determine.

citation.title: The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Even about two drinks reduce REM; the 'drowsy' effect (faster sleep onset) only appeared around five drinks. Supports the myth line.
notes: No conflicts declared. The abstract does not report a timing-specific cutoff, so it does not by itself support '3 hours before bed'.

question: What does alcohol do to sleep in healthy people?
population: healthy volunteers (all known studies, qualitative review)
keyResult: At all doses alcohol shortened sleep onset latency, consolidated the first half of sleep, and increased sleep disruption in the second half. Delayed onset of the first REM period occurred at all doses; total-night REM % decreased in most studies at moderate and high doses. Slow-wave sleep increased in the first half of the night.

citation.title: Alcohol and sleep I: effects on normal sleep.

notes: Landmark qualitative review (pre-2015). Describes the 'sleepy early, broken later' pattern behind the myth line.

question: Does evening alcohol affect the body's recovery during the first hours of sleep in real life?
keyResult: Alcohol was dose-dependently associated with increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic regulation in the first 3 hours of sleep, even at low intake (all P<.001). HRV-derived recovery decreased on average by 9.3, 24.0 and 39.2 percentage units with low (≤0.25 g/kg), moderate (>0.25-0.75 g/kg) and high (>0.75 g/kg) intake.

citation.title: Acute Effect of Alcohol Intake on Cardiovascular Autonomic Regulation During the First Hours of Sleep in a Large Real-World Sample of Finnish Employees: Observational Study.

notes: COI: some authors employed by Firstbeat Technologies (HRV device maker) and Nokia. Measures heart physiology, not sleep stages. Does not test how many hours before bed to stop.

question: Does medical cannabis improve sleep in adults with insomnia?
keyResult: Compared with placebo, medical cannabis may have little to no clinically meaningful effect on sleep quality/satisfaction (SMD -0.49, 95%CI -1.06 to 0.08; very low certainty), total sleep time (MD 7.68 minutes, 95% CI -23.04 to 38.39; very low certainty) or daytime functioning, and may result in a slight increase in adverse events (OR 11.25, 95% CI 4.46 to 28.35; low certainty).

citation.title: Medical cannabis for the treatment of insomnia.

notes: Cochrane review with meta-analysis; no dedicated funding; authors declare no relevant conflicts. Mostly female participants (72.66%).

question: What does cannabis do to sleep architecture measured by polysomnography?
keyResult: Cannabis administration did not consistently alter sleep duration, latency, wake time, efficiency or staging. Early reports of reduced REM came from small, high-THC studies; newer studies show mixed and often no REM suppression. Withdrawal from regular use was consistently associated with disturbed sleep: less total sleep, longer sleep onset latency and REM rebound.

citation.title: Cannabis and sleep architecture: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Evidence base small. Withdrawal finding supports a line that stopping regular use can disturb sleep for a while.

question: What doses and forms of cannabis affect sleep?
keyResult: Sleep improved in 7 of 19 randomized studies and 7 of 12 uncontrolled trials. No significant differences between THC and CBD. Benefits mostly in pain-related conditions; no significant effects in healthy participants. Subjective improvements were common but objective sleep architecture did not improve. Adverse events (headache, sedation, dizziness) were more frequent at higher doses.

citation.title: Cannabis dosing and administration for sleep: a systematic review.

notes: Covers both THC and CBD; no dosing recommendation possible.

question: Is cannabis use within 3 hours of sleep linked to different sleep architecture?
keyResult: Cannabis use within 3 hours of sleep was associated with more wake after sleep onset (median 60.5 vs 45.8 minutes; rate ratio 1.59) and a higher proportion of stage 1 sleep (median 15.2% vs 12.3%). Frequent users (>20 days per month) also had more wake, longer REM latency and lower sleep efficiency. No association with longer or more efficient sleep.

citation.title: The impact of cannabis use proximal to sleep and cannabinoid metabolites on sleep architecture.

notes: Cross-sectional (studyType closest is cohort/other); one-night home test; state public-health grant funding. Supports 'keep it away from bedtime'.

question: Should medical cannabis be used to treat obstructive sleep apnea?
keyResult: AASM position: medical cannabis and/or its synthetic extracts should not be used to treat OSA because of unreliable delivery methods and insufficient evidence of effectiveness, tolerability and safety; patients should discuss treatment options with a licensed provider at an accredited sleep facility.

citation.title: Medical Cannabis and the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Position Statement.

notes: Position statement; useful for a caveat line: 'cannabis is not a treatment for snoring or sleep apnea'.

newAdvice: Avoid nicotine (smoking or vaping), especially in the evening; it is linked to lighter, shorter sleep.
question: Do chronic tobacco smokers sleep differently from non-smokers?
population: chronic smokers without comorbidities vs healthy controls (14 studies, 10 meta-analysed)
keyResult: Smokers had more N1 (SMD = 0.65) and N2 (SMD = 1.45), more wake after sleep onset (SMD = 6.37, 95%CI 2.48 to 10.26) and less slow-wave sleep (SMD = -2.00, 95%CI -3.30 to -0.70) than controls, mostly in the first part of the night. Subjective PSQI did not differ significantly (SMD = 0.53, 95%CI -0.18 to 1.23).

citation.title: Tobacco-induced sleep disturbances: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: No conflicts declared. Case-control comparisons (not experiments on evening nicotine timing). No current concept covers nicotine.

newAdvice: Avoid nicotine (smoking or vaping), especially in the evening; it is linked to lighter, shorter sleep.
question: Does smoking predict later sleep problems?
keyResult: Smokers had a higher risk of developing sleep-related issues than non-smokers (risk ratio 1.47; 1.20-1.79). Egger's and Begg's tests indicated publication bias.

citation.title: Smoking and risk of sleep-related issues: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies.

notes: Observational; publication bias reported. No conflicts declared.

newAdvice: Avoid nicotine (smoking or vaping), especially in the evening; it is linked to lighter, shorter sleep.
question: Is e-cigarette use linked to shorter or worse sleep?
keyResult: E-cigarette users had higher odds of short sleep duration than non-users (pooled OR 1.38, 95% CI: 1.24-1.55). Among adolescents, e-cigarette use was associated with a 33 to 61% increased risk of inadequate sleep.

citation.title: Impact of electronic cigarette use and sleep duration, sleep issues and insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: All cross-sectional; cannot show cause. No conflicts declared.

question: Does eating dinner 1 hour vs 5 hours before bed change sleep?
keyResult: Conventional sleep stages were similar after late dinner (1 h before bed) and routine dinner (5 h before bed). Late dinner caused a 2.5% initial increase in delta power and a 2.7% decrease in alpha+beta power (p<0.0001), reversing later in the night. The authors conclude late dinner did not cause significant adverse changes in sleep architecture.

citation.title: Effects of Dinner Timing on Sleep Stage Distribution and EEG Power Spectrum in Healthy Volunteers.

disagreement: Disagrees with Enomoto 2026, which found worse sleep continuity after a dinner 1 h before bed. Small studies point in different directions.
notes: Post hoc analysis; single night; isocaloric meal; no conflicts declared.

question: Does eating dinner 1 hour before bed for several days affect sleep in young women?
population: 13 healthy young women, real-life crossover, 4 days per condition
keyResult: On day 4, dinner 1 h before bedtime (vs 5 h) gave significantly shorter total sleep time (p = 0.013), lower sleep efficiency (p = 0.040), more wake after sleep onset (p = 0.017) and more arousals and stage shifts. Only transient changes in post-meal glucose were seen.

citation.title: Effects of later dinner timing on subsequent metabolic function and nocturnal sleep in healthy young women.

disagreement: Disagrees with Duan 2021 (one night, no adverse change).
notes: Very small sample (n=13), women only; dinner 709-740 kcal. No competing interests declared.

question: What lifestyle measures does the ACG recommend for GERD, including meal timing?
keyResult: 'We suggest avoiding meals within 2-3 hours of bedtime' (conditional recommendation, low level of evidence). The text notes that a short interval (<3 hours) between eating and bedtime or lying down is associated with more GERD symptoms.

citation.title: ACG Clinical Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease.

notes: Read the guideline's recommendation list in the PMC full text. Applies to people with reflux; supports the 'food 2 hours' part of the 3-2-1 rule for this group.

question: Do the amount and type of carbohydrate affect sleep?
population: 11 articles, 27 nutrition trials, mostly healthy adults
keyResult: Compared with high carbohydrate intake, low carbohydrate intake moderately increased N3 duration (ES = 0.37) and proportion (ES = 0.51). High carbohydrate intake prolonged REM duration (ES = -0.38) and proportion (ES = -0.46). Carbohydrate quality (glycemic index) did not affect sleep stages; changes in glycemic load explained part of the variance in sleep onset latency (R2 = 50.8), sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset.

citation.title: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression on the Effects of Carbohydrates on Sleep.

disagreement: No clear support for 'a high-carb snack helps you sleep'; effects run both ways depending on sleep stage.
notes: No conflicts declared. Short-term trials only.

question: Does a high-glycemic-index meal shorten sleep onset, and does timing matter?
keyResult: A high-GI rice meal 4 h before bedtime reduced sleep onset latency to 9.0 ± 6.2 min vs 17.5 ± 6.2 min with a low-GI meal (P = 0.009). The same high-GI meal given 1 h before bedtime gave 14.6 ± 9.9 min (P = 0.01 vs 4 h). No effects on other sleep variables.

citation.title: High-glycemic-index carbohydrate meals shorten sleep onset.

disagreement: Often cited for 'carbs before bed'; but the benefit was at 4 h before bed, not as a bedtime snack.
notes: Tiny sample, men only, very high-carbohydrate (90.4% energy) test meal. Pre-2015.

question: Does eating two kiwifruit before bed improve sleep?
population: 24 adults aged 20-55 with self-reported sleep problems (22 women)
keyResult: After 4 weeks of 2 kiwifruit 1 hour before bedtime, PSQI score, wake after sleep onset and sleep onset latency decreased by 42.4%, 28.9% and 35.4%; total sleep time and sleep efficiency increased by 13.4% and 5.41%.

citation.title: Effect of kiwifruit consumption on sleep quality in adults with sleep problems.

notes: Uncontrolled before-after study (no placebo or control group); small; funded research (non-US government per PubMed). No DOI on PubMed record.

question: Does tart cherry improve sleep?
keyResult: Three of seven studies reported significant improvements in sleep (duration, efficiency or onset time); three reported higher melatonin levels. Large differences in dose, duration and populations; evidence described as limited and heterogeneous.

citation.title: The Effect of Tart Cherry on Sleep Quality and Sleep Disorders: A Systematic Review.

notes: No conflicts declared. Small evidence base.

question: Does tart cherry juice concentrate raise melatonin and improve sleep?
keyResult: Total urinary melatonin was significantly elevated with cherry juice (P < 0.05), and time in bed, total sleep time and sleep efficiency increased significantly (P < 0.05) compared with placebo.

citation.title: Effect of tart cherry juice (Prunus cerasus) on melatonin levels and enhanced sleep quality.

notes: Small, healthy volunteers, 1 week. Pre-2015.

question: Do foods that naturally contain melatonin improve sleep?
keyResult: Interventional studies suggested melatonin-rich foods (Montmorency tart cherries, Jerte Valley cherries, tomatoes, kiwifruit) may improve sleep quality, duration and efficiency, particularly in people with sleep disturbances, but findings were heterogeneous and studies varied in dose, timing and measurement.

citation.title: Effectiveness of Melatonin-Containing Foods on Promoting Sleep: A Scoping Review.

notes: Scoping review (no pooled estimate). No conflicts declared. Supports keeping the 'small studies' hedge in the plain line.

question: Does oral magnesium help older adults with insomnia?
population: older adults with insomnia; 3 RCTs, 151 participants
keyResult: Sleep onset latency was 17.36 min shorter with magnesium than placebo (95% CI -27.27 to -7.44, p = 0.0006). Total sleep time improved by 16.06 min but was not statistically significant. All trials had moderate-to-high risk of bias; evidence low to very low quality.

citation.title: Oral magnesium supplementation for insomnia in older adults: a Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis.

notes: Older adults only; only 3 small trials. None declared.

question: Does magnesium supplementation improve sleep in adults?
population: adults; 12 RCTs in main synthesis (plus 3 on cramps/RLS)
keyResult: Findings were inconsistent across subjective outcomes, EEG, actigraphy, wearables and physiological markers; certainty low to very low. The authors conclude current evidence does not support oral magnesium as a routine treatment for insomnia, though it may give modest benefits for some subjective outcomes in some adults.

citation.title: Magnesium Supplementation for Sleep in Adults: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.

notes: Most recent review (searched to 1 June 2026). Narrative synthesis, no pooling. COI not shown in the PubMed abstract; first author has published industry-funded supplement trials, check full text. Consistent with current plain line ('ask before taking a supplement').

question: Does chamomile improve sleep?
keyResult: Chamomile significantly reduced PSQI score (WMD: -1.88, 95% CI: -3.46, -0.31, I2: 88.4%, n = 5). Sleep onset latency improved in three of four studies and night awakenings in two of three; sleep efficiency and daytime functioning did not improve. No adverse events reported.

citation.title: Effects of chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla L.) on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials.

notes: High heterogeneity; most trials used extracts or capsules rather than tea; only one study checked blinding and product purity. No competing interests declared.

question: Does passionflower extract improve objective sleep in insomnia disorder?
population: 110 adults with DSM-5 insomnia disorder, 2 weeks
keyResult: Total sleep time on polysomnography increased more with passionflower than placebo (23.05 ± 54.26 vs -0.16 ± 53.12 min; P = 0.049). Sleep efficiency and WASO improved within the passionflower group but not compared with placebo.

citation.title: Effects of Passiflora incarnata Linnaeus on polysomnographic sleep parameters in subjects with insomnia disorder: a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled study.

notes: Extract, not tea. Borderline significance (P = 0.049); short trial.

question: Does passionflower tea improve subjective sleep quality?
keyResult: Of six sleep-diary measures, only sleep quality was rated significantly better with passionflower tea than placebo tea (t(40) = 2.70, p < 0.01).

citation.title: A double-blind, placebo-controlled investigation of the effects of Passiflora incarnata (passionflower) herbal tea on subjective sleep quality.

notes: Small; only 1 of 6 outcomes improved; pre-2015. Supports passionflower as an option alongside chamomile.

question: How should nocturia (waking at night to urinate) be managed?
keyResult: Lifestyle changes and treating underlying conditions are first-line. Limiting fluid intake, especially in the evening, adjusting the timing of diuretics, and sleep hygiene are recommended; bladder diaries help diagnosis.

citation.title: Nocturia: Evaluation and Management.

notes: Clinical review, not a guideline. Note: nocturia can signal other conditions (including sleep apnea), so persistent nocturia warrants a check.

question: What is a practical approach to nocturia?
keyResult: Expert recommendations: lifestyle changes (e.g., reducing evening fluid intake) are the first intervention; diuretics should be taken mid-late afternoon. Clinically relevant nocturia (≥2 voids per night) affects 2%-18% of those aged 20-40 years, rising to 28%-62% at 70-80 years.

citation.title: A practical approach to the management of nocturia.

notes: Expert consensus; check full text for industry sponsorship (desmopressin is discussed).

question: Does regular exercise improve sleep quality and insomnia in adults?
keyResult: Exercise improved subjective sleep: PSQI (MD -2.19; 95% CI -2.96 to -1.41), ISI (MD -1.52; 95% CI -2.63 to -0.41) and ESS (MD -2.55; 95% CI -3.32 to -1.78). Physical and mind-body exercise improved PSQI to a similar extent. Few objective (actigraphy) effects except higher sleep efficiency.

citation.title: Effects of Exercise on Sleep Quality and Insomnia in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

notes: No conflicts declared. Mostly self-reported benefits.

question: Which types and doses of exercise best improve sleep quality?
keyResult: All six exercise types improved sleep quality vs control: aerobic (SMD = -1.21), resistance (SMD = -1.12), combined (SMD = -1.11), yoga (SMD = -0.82), Pilates (SMD = -1.65), traditional Chinese exercise (SMD = -0.94). The dose-response was U-shaped, with an overall optimum of 920 MET-min/week.

citation.title: The best approaches and doses of exercise for improving sleep quality: a network meta-analysis and dose-response relationship study.

notes: No competing interests declared. 920 MET-min/week is roughly 230 min/week of moderate activity at 4 METs (our arithmetic, not stated in abstract; verify before use). Very large SMDs suggest heterogeneity.

question: Does exercise help people with insomnia disorder?
population: people with insomnia disorder (umbrella review + network meta-analysis, 1034 participants)
keyResult: Various exercise types improved total sleep time and sleep quality and reduced insomnia severity. Moderate aerobic exercise, mind-body exercise, and moderate aerobic plus light strength training improved objectively measured sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset.

citation.title: The effects of exercise on insomnia disorders: An umbrella review and network meta-analysis.

notes: Included systematic reviews were of (very) low methodological quality. No competing interests declared.

question: Does evening exercise harm sleep?
population: healthy adults; 23 studies of a single evening exercise session
keyResult: Evening exercise increased REM latency (+7.7 min) and slow-wave sleep (+1.3 percentage points) and decreased stage 1 sleep (-0.9 pp). Overall the studies do not support the idea that evening exercise harms sleep, rather the opposite; however, sleep onset latency, total sleep time and sleep efficiency might be impaired after vigorous exercise ending ≤ 1 h before bedtime.

citation.title: Effects of Evening Exercise on Sleep in Healthy Participants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

disagreement: Supports the narrow version of the line (vigorous, within about 1 h) but not a general ban on evening exercise. 'A couple of hours' in the current line is slightly more cautious than this evidence.
notes: Moderator effects disappeared after removing one study. Healthy, mostly young adults.

question: Does evening high-intensity exercise disrupt sleep?
population: healthy good sleepers aged 18-50; 15 acute studies, 194 participants
keyResult: Acute evening high-intensity exercise ending 0.5-4 h before bedtime decreased REM sleep (-2.34%; p = 0.002) vs no exercise; no other significant sleep changes. Regular evening high-intensity exercise did not disrupt sleep. Acute high-intensity exercise performed 2-4 h before bedtime does not disrupt sleep.

citation.title: The effects of evening high-intensity exercise on sleep in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Consistent with the current plain line (finish hard workouts at least a couple of hours before bed) and with the myth line.
notes: No conflicts declared. Good sleepers only; may not apply to people with insomnia.

question: Does the time of day of exercise change its effect on sleep?
keyResult: Direct time-vs-time comparisons for sleep were non-significant (g = 0.15, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.39], p = 0.209), with no stable advantage for morning, afternoon or evening exercise. Authors conclude exercise itself may matter more than its timing for sleep.

citation.title: Time-of-day effects of acute and regular exercise on sleep quality and mood: a three-level meta-analysis.

disagreement: No evidence found for a specific best time for strength training; the current line ('afternoon or early evening') is not supported or contradicted by a direct study. Consider replacing with 'any time that fits, but not a hard session right before bed'.
notes: Not specific to resistance training; few studies. No conflicts declared.

question: Does resistance exercise improve sleep?
keyResult: Chronic resistance exercise improved all aspects of sleep, with the greatest benefit for sleep quality; acute effects were poorly studied and inconsistent. The authors call for studies on time-of-day and dose-response effects.

citation.title: The effect of resistance exercise on sleep: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials.

disagreement: Supports doing strength training for sleep but says nothing on timing; the timing part of the line has no evidence base here.
notes: Direction 'mixed' because it supports strength training but not the timing claim.

question: Does yoga improve sleep in women with sleep problems?
population: women with sleep problems; 19 studies, 1832 participants
keyResult: Yoga improved sleep overall (SMD = -0.327, 95% CI -0.506 to -0.148) and PSQI (SMD = -0.54; 95% CI -0.89 to -0.19; 16 RCTs), but showed no effect on insomnia severity (ISI; SMD = -0.13), and no effect in breast cancer or peri/postmenopausal subgroups. No serious adverse events.

citation.title: The effect of yoga on sleep quality and insomnia in women with sleep problems: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Studies tested yoga programmes, not a few minutes of stretching at bedtime; no good trial of bedtime stretching was found.
notes: Women only. No competing interests declared.

question: Does a warm bath or shower before bed improve sleep?
keyResult: Water-based passive body heating at 40-42.5 °C was associated with better self-rated sleep quality and sleep efficiency, and when scheduled 1-2 h before bedtime for as little as 10 min, significantly shorter sleep onset latency.

citation.title: Before-bedtime passive body heating by warm shower or bath to improve sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Limited number of studies; optimal timing and duration not settled. Matches the current plain line (1-2 h before bed).

question: Is higher ambient temperature linked to worse sleep in real-world settings?
keyResult: Higher outdoor or indoor temperatures were generally associated with worse sleep quality and quantity, with stronger effects in the hottest months and days, in vulnerable populations and in the warmest regions; limited evidence of fast adaptation to heat.

citation.title: A systematic review of ambient heat and sleep in a warming climate.

notes: No conflicts declared. Observational.

question: What bedroom temperature is linked to the best sleep in older adults at home?
population: community-dwelling older adults, longitudinal, wearables and room sensors
keyResult: Sleep was most efficient and restful at nighttime bedroom temperatures between 20 and 25 °C, with a clinically relevant 5-10 % drop in sleep efficiency when temperature rose from 25 °C to 30 °C. Associations were nonlinear with large differences between people.

citation.title: Nighttime ambient temperature and sleep in community-dwelling older adults.

disagreement: 20-25 °C (68-77 °F) is warmer than the 15.6-19.4 °C (60-67 °F) range often quoted in popular advice. 'Cool' should mean 'not hot', adjusted to the person.
notes: Older adults only; observational. No competing interests declared.

question: How does the thermal environment affect sleep?
population: narrative review of lab and field studies
keyResult: Heat or cold exposure increases wakefulness and decreases REM and slow-wave sleep. With normal bedding and clothing, heat exposure increases wakefulness and decreases slow-wave and REM sleep, and humid heat adds further load; cold exposure does not affect sleep stages when bedding and clothing are used, though it affects cardiac autonomic responses.

citation.title: Effects of thermal environment on sleep and circadian rhythm.

notes: Narrative review, pre-2015. Supports avoiding a hot bedroom; with bedding, a cooler room is tolerated.

question: How should people deal with sleep problems during heatwaves?
population: general population and vulnerable groups (European Insomnia Network)
keyResult: Reviews how higher night-time temperatures affect body temperature and sleep, especially in older adults, children, pregnant women and people with psychiatric conditions, and gives practical advice adapted from CBT-I elements. Notes the literature is sparse.

citation.title: How to deal with sleep problems during heatwaves: practical recommendations from the European Insomnia Network.

notes: The specific practical tips (e.g. cooling methods) are in the full text, not the abstract; read before citing for the frozen-water-bottle tip.

question: Does bedding that cools the body improve sleep?
keyResult: With very low to low certainty, cooling bedding strategies (mattress, topper, pillow) showed no differences vs control in sleep onset latency, sleep efficiency, sleep stages, wake after sleep onset or total sleep time, although some studies showed acute lowering of core body temperature (p < 0.05).

citation.title: Does body cooling facilitated by bedding compared to control condition improve sleep among adults (18-64 years old)? A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: No study of the frozen-water-bottle trick was found; the closest evidence (cooling bedding) shows no sleep benefit in healthy adults in normal conditions.
notes: Not tested in hot conditions or heatwaves, where cooling would be expected to matter more. No competing interests declared.

question: Do bed socks improve sleep in a cool room?
keyResult: With feet-warming bed socks, sleep onset latency was on average 7.5 min shorter, total sleep time 32 min longer, number of awakenings 7.5 times smaller and sleep efficiency 7.6% higher (all P < 0.05); foot temperature was 1.3 °C higher. No difference in subjective sleep ratings.

citation.title: Effects of feet warming using bed socks on sleep quality and thermoregulatory responses in a cool environment.

notes: Only 6 participants, all young men; actigraphy. Small mechanistic study.

question: Does continuous white or broadband noise help sleep?
keyResult: Findings varied from continuous noise improving sleep to disrupting it. Under GRADE, the quality of evidence that continuous noise improves sleep was very low, which contradicts its widespread use; authors caution it may also harm sleep and hearing.

citation.title: Noise as a sleep aid: A systematic review.

disagreement: Disagrees with the current support score of 3 for steady sound; evidence is very low quality.
notes: No conflicts declared.

question: Does white noise improve sleep across age groups and settings?
population: 12 RCTs, 1301 participants (infants, adults, older adults; ICU and non-ICU)
keyResult: White noise lowered PSQI scores in adults (MD = -3.70, 95% CI -4.90 to -2.50) and older adults (MD = -2.71, 95% CI -4.98 to -0.44), and in both ICU (MD = -4.04) and non-ICU (MD = -2.61) patients. In infants it lengthened 24-h total sleep time (MD = 137.51 min) but not nocturnal 12-h total sleep time.

citation.title: Impact of white noise on sleep quality across age groups and in critically ill/non-critically ill patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

disagreement: More positive than Riedy 2021, but many trials were in hospital/ICU settings and quality was limited.
notes: Substantial heterogeneity; many hospital patients (ICU caveat). Abstract partly written in future tense (protocol wording). No competing interests declared.

question: Do white or pink noise devices improve sleep in adults?
keyResult: 19 studies had positive findings: 6 of 18 white noise (33%), 9 of 11 pink noise (81.9%) and 4 of 6 multiaudio (66.7%). Authors found no strong evidence to support auditory stimulation; no adverse effects reported with short-term use.

citation.title: Systematic review: auditory stimulation and sleep.

disagreement: Vote-counting favours pink noise, but see Basner 2026 RCT showing pink noise reduced REM sleep.
notes: No conflicts declared. Mixed study quality.

question: Do pink noise and earplugs protect sleep from intermittent environmental noise?
keyResult: Environmental noise reduced N3 deep sleep (p < .0001), while pink noise (40 or 50 dBA) reduced REM sleep (p < .001). Adding pink noise to environmental noise worsened sleep structure despite minor improvements in fragmentation. Earplugs mitigated nearly all environmental noise effects but started failing at 65 dBA. Authors caution against widespread, indiscriminate use of broadband noise.

citation.title: Efficacy of pink noise and earplugs for mitigating the effects of intermittent environmental noise exposure on sleep.

disagreement: Contradicts the current pink-noise line and the steady-sound line; favours earplugs (keep-the-bedroom-quiet) over masking sound.
notes: Small lab study (n=25, mostly women: 7 male); continuous all-night pink noise, not phase-locked stimulation. Registered NCT05774977. COI not in abstract.

question: Do earplugs protect sleep from traffic-type noise?
keyResult: Earplugs mitigated nearly all effects of intermittent environmental noise on sleep, but started failing at the highest noise level (65 dBA). Pink noise, by contrast, reduced REM sleep.

citation.title: Efficacy of pink noise and earplugs for mitigating the effects of intermittent environmental noise exposure on sleep.

notes: Same study as the pink-noise entry; listed twice because it bears on two concepts.

question: Do non-drug measures such as earplugs and eye masks help sleep in the ICU?
population: critically ill adults in ICU; 30 trials, 1569 participants
keyResult: Earplugs and/or eye masks were linked to lower delirium incidence (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.80; 2 studies, 177 participants) and longer total sleep time (mean difference 2.19 hours, 95% CI 0.41 to 3.96; 2 studies, 116 participants), both low-quality evidence. Most studies of earplugs and eye masks found no benefit on objective sleep.

citation.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for sleep promotion in the intensive care unit.

notes: ICU CAVEAT: hospital ICU patients, a very different noise and light setting from a home bedroom. Use only as indirect support.

question: Do earplugs and eye masks improve sleep quality in ICU patients?
keyResult: Overall effect on self-reported sleep quality SMD 1.44 (95% CI 0.80, 2.09). Earplugs alone had no significant effect (0.07, 95% CI -0.50, 0.64); eye masks alone had a significant effect (1.56, 95% CI 1.08, 2.05); both together had the largest effect (2.08, 95% CI 0.95, 3.21).

citation.title: Effect of earplugs and eye masks on the sleep quality of intensive care unit patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: In ICU, eye masks helped but earplugs alone did not; in Basner 2026 (healthy adults, home-like noise) earplugs helped. Setting matters.
notes: ICU CAVEAT: hospital ICU patients only; not directly applicable to home bedrooms.

question: Which mattress type best supports sleep quality and reduces back pain?
population: adults with or without back pain; 24 controlled trials
keyResult: A mattress subjectively described as medium-firm and custom inflated (self-adjusted) was optimal for sleep comfort, quality and spinal alignment. Evidence on the best mattress temperature was insufficient.

citation.title: Effect of different mattress designs on promoting sleep quality, pain reduction, and spinal alignment in adults with or without back pain; systematic review of controlled trials.

notes: Firmness categories were subjective. Industry funding of underlying mattress trials not assessed in abstract.

question: What type of mattress should be chosen to avoid back pain and improve sleep quality?
keyResult: A medium-firm mattress promoted comfort, sleep quality and spinal alignment.

citation.title: What type of mattress should be chosen to avoid back pain and improve sleep quality? Review of the literature.

notes: No financial conflicts reported. Consistent with Radwan 2015.

question: Do pillow designs change neck pain or sleep quality?
population: adults, mostly with chronic neck pain; 35 articles (9 high-quality, 555 participants)
keyResult: Rubber pillows reduced neck pain (SMD: -0.263), waking pain (SMD: -0.228) and neck disability (SMD: -0.506), and pillow use increased satisfaction (SMD: 1.144), but pillow design did not influence sleep quality (SMD = 0.047; P = 0.703) in people with chronic neck pain.

citation.title: The effects of pillow designs on neck pain, waking symptoms, neck disability, sleep quality and spinal alignment in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Supports 'a pillow that feels comfortable to you' rather than any specific pillow product.
notes: Neck-pain population.

question: Do weighted chain blankets reduce insomnia in psychiatric patients?
population: 120 patients with major depression, bipolar disorder, generalized anxiety disorder or ADHD; 4 weeks
keyResult: At 4 weeks, the weighted blanket group had significantly better Insomnia Severity Index ratings than the light blanket group (P < .001; Cohen's d 1.90), with better sleep maintenance, higher daytime activity and less fatigue, depression and anxiety. No serious adverse events; effects held over 12 months of open follow-up.

citation.title: A randomized controlled study of weighted chain blankets for insomnia in psychiatric disorders.

notes: Psychiatric outpatients only; participants could feel which blanket they had (hard to blind). Check full text for any funding or COI with the blanket maker.

question: What is the evidence on weighted blanket use?
keyResult: Weighted blankets may help reduce anxiety, but there is not enough evidence that they help with insomnia.

citation.title: Weighted Blanket Use: A Systematic Review.

notes: Search ended March 2018, before the Ekholm 2020 RCT.

question: What are the outcomes of overnight weighted blanket use?
keyResult: Adults reported improved sleep, less medication use and better mood; sleep outcomes were mixed for children and adolescents. Methodological quality was variable and no guidelines for use exist.

citation.title: Weighted Blankets as a Sleep Intervention: A Scoping Review.

notes: Scoping review; no pooled effect. Current hedge ('some people find...') fits.

question: Does lavender essential oil improve sleep in adults?
keyResult: Lavender essential oil improved sleep quality (standardized mean difference = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.96, -0.17], P = .005); authors note the conclusion needs verification in higher-quality studies.

citation.title: The Sleep-Enhancing Effect of Lavender Essential Oil in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

notes: Limited number and quality of studies; mixed populations (many clinical).

question: Does aromatherapy improve sleep quality in adults and older people?
keyResult: Overall effect size on sleep quality was 0.74. Larger effects in East Asian studies (1.02), quasi-experimental studies (1.24) and aroma massage studies (1.30).

citation.title: Effect of aromatherapy on sleep quality of adults and elderly people: A systematic literature review and meta-analysis.

notes: Larger effects in less rigorous (quasi-experimental) designs and when combined with massage suggest bias and confounding; blinding a scent is hard.

question: Does aromatherapy improve sleep quality in older adults?
keyResult: Aromatherapy improved sleep quality (SMD = -1.02; 95% CI -1.38 to -0.66); lavender alone SMD = -1.39 (95% CI -2.06 to -0.72); non-inhaled aromatherapy SMD = -1.73.

citation.title: Effects of aromatherapy on sleep quality in older adults: A meta-analysis.

notes: Older adults only; non-inhaled (massage) forms showed the largest effect, which may not reflect scent alone. No conflicts declared.

question: Is mouth taping safe and effective for mouth breathing, snoring or sleep apnea?
population: 10 studies, 213 patients with mouth breathing, sleep-disordered breathing or OSA
keyResult: Two studies showed significant improvement in sleep apnea markers (AHI or oxygen desaturation); others showed no difference and discussed risks including asphyxiation with nasal obstruction. Many studies excluded people with nasal obstruction. Authors see a potentially serious risk of harm for people taping indiscriminately.

citation.title: Breaking social media fads and uncovering the safety and efficacy of mouth taping in patients with mouth breathing, sleep disordered breathing, or obstructive sleep apnea: A systematic review.

disagreement: Supports the current hedge ('evidence is thin; check with a clinician first'). This is the 2025 systematic review the brief asked about.
notes: No competing interests declared.

question: How do nasal obstruction and mouth taping affect sleep apnea?
population: studies of induced or post-surgical nasal obstruction; 2 mouth-taping studies reviewed narratively
keyResult: Nasal obstruction increased AHI by +13.78 events/h and ODI by +7.45 events/h. Two small mouth-taping studies reported reduced AHI in mild OSA (no meta-analysis possible).

citation.title: Impact of Nasal Obstruction and Mouth Taping on Sleep Apnea Indicators: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

notes: Supports the importance of a clear nose; also relevant to nose-breathing-exercises (but not about breathing exercises). COI: none.

question: Does mouth tape improve CPAP adherence in mouth-breathing OSA patients?
population: 62 patients with OSA on CPAP who mouth-breathe; crossover, 30 days each
keyResult: With mouth tape, average CPAP use rose by 51.8 minutes per day (95% CI 33.1-70.4); 17.6% more days reached ≥4 hours/night; odds ratio for good adherence 4.5. Sleepiness, snoring, mouth dryness and night awakenings improved. Adverse effects were reported.

citation.title: The role of mouth tape for CPAP use in patients with mouth breathing and OSA.

disagreement: Benefit is under clinical supervision with CPAP, not as a stand-alone home remedy.
notes: CPAP users only; no conflicts declared.

question: Does sleeping on the left side reduce night-time reflux?
keyResult: Left-side sleeping reduced acid exposure time vs right side (MD -2.03) and vs supine (MD -2.71) and shortened acid clearance time; one RCT of a positional device improved night-time symptoms and reflux-free nights.

citation.title: Left lateral decubitus sleeping position is associated with improved gastroesophageal reflux disease symptoms: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Very few studies. No conflicts declared.

question: Does a wearable that discourages right-side sleeping reduce nocturnal reflux symptoms?
population: 100 patients with nocturnal GERD symptoms; double-blind sham-controlled
keyResult: Treatment success (≥50% fall in nocturnal reflux score) was 44% with the device vs 24% with sham (risk difference 20%; 95% CI 1.8%-38.2%; P = .03). Time on the left side rose to 60.9% vs 38.5%; reflux-free nights 9 vs 6.

citation.title: Sleep Positional Therapy for Nocturnal Gastroesophageal Reflux: A Double-Blind, Randomized, Sham-Controlled Trial.

notes: COI not in abstract; check full text (device study).

question: Should people with night-time reflux raise the head of the bed?
keyResult: 'We suggest elevating head of bed for nighttime GERD symptoms' (conditional recommendation, low level of evidence). The text notes several RCTs showed improvement in nocturnal symptoms and acid exposure with head-of-bed elevation or a wedge, and that lying right-side down increases nocturnal reflux compared with left-side down.

citation.title: ACG Clinical Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease.

notes: Read the recommendation list in PMC full text. Also supports left-side-for-reflux.

question: Which interventions work for nocturnal reflux?
keyResult: Lifestyle studies included head-of-bed elevation (n = 5), longer dinner-to-bed time (n = 2) and left-side positioning (n = 2). Authors recommend a stepwise strategy: head-of-bed elevation, longer dinner-to-bed interval, left-side sleeping, then acid-suppressive medicine.

citation.title: Systematic review: Clinical effectiveness of interventions for the treatment of nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux.

notes: COI: two authors report industry funding/fees (Boston Scientific, Cook, Olympus; Nutricia, Norgine, Medtronic and others).

question: Does a mild head-of-bed elevation reduce obstructive sleep apnea severity?
population: 52 OSA patients, single clinic, before-after polysomnography
keyResult: Head-of-bed elevation of 7.5° lowered AHI from 15.7 [11.3-22.5] to 10.7 [6.6-16.5] events/h (p < 0.001) and raised minimum oxygen saturation from 83.5 to 87% (p = 0.003), without changing sleep architecture.

citation.title: The influence of head-of-bed elevation in patients with obstructive sleep apnea.

notes: Uncontrolled, single night; moderate reduction, not a substitute for treatment. No conflicts declared. A 2022 study (Iannella, PMID 36233488) found AHI fell from 23.8 to 17.7 at 30° elevation.

question: How should adults with suspected sleep apnea be tested?
population: adults with signs and symptoms of OSA
keyResult: AASM: polysomnography is the standard test when a comprehensive sleep evaluation raises concern for OSA. Questionnaires and prediction tools should not be used to diagnose OSA without polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing (STRONG). Polysomnography or a technically adequate home test is recommended for uncomplicated adults with signs and symptoms of moderate-to-severe OSA (STRONG).

citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for Diagnostic Testing for Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline.

notes: Supports 'ask a doctor' for people with symptoms; online quizzes are not a diagnosis.

question: Should adults without symptoms be screened for sleep apnea?
population: asymptomatic adults and adults with unrecognized symptoms
keyResult: USPSTF: current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for OSA in the general adult population (I statement). Estimated prevalence of moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI ≥15) was 13% in men and 6% in women.

citation.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force (Mangione CM, et al.)
citation.title: Screening for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.

disagreement: Not a conflict with the plain line: the line targets people who already snore loudly or gasp (symptomatic), which is outside USPSTF's screening scope.
notes: Authors field empty in PubMed record (task-force statement).

newAdvice: If your snoring or apnea is worse on your back, sleeping on your side may help; ask your clinician.
question: Does positional therapy (staying off your back) help obstructive sleep apnea?
keyResult: Compared with inactive control, positional therapy improved sleepiness (ESS MD -1.58) and reduced AHI (MD -7.38 events per hour; low certainty). CPAP reduced AHI more than positional therapy (MD 6.4 events per hour), but self-reported adherence was higher with positional therapy (MD 2.5 hours per night; moderate certainty).

citation.title: Positional therapy for obstructive sleep apnoea.

notes: Short studies; positional OSA only. Advice must route through a clinician because CPAP works better.
